Consult Summary:
- 34-year-old male (Jack Smith, DOB 31-Oct-1990) with ~6 weeks of progressive, intermittent left-sided hearing reduction with intermittent left-sided tinnitus and occasional mild dizziness/nausea; plan made for in-person otoscopic ear exam to exclude cerumen impaction as first-line evaluation.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Progressive decrease in hearing in the left ear for approximately six weeks.
  - Intermittent left-sided tinnitus (ringing).
  - Occasional mild dizziness/lightheadedness with some nausea; described as off-balance rather than true rotational vertigo.
  - Patient reports a prior brief (couple-day) episode of hearing difficulty about one year ago.

- Timeline / progression:
  - Symptoms began ~6 weeks ago.
  - Symptoms are intermittent (on and off) during this period and described as gradually present over weeks.
  - Some symptom relief of the tinnitus when exposed to external sound (watching TV, listening to music).

- Exacerbating / relieving factors:
  - External sound (TV/music) tends to mask/relieve tinnitus.
  - Patient statements about ear cleaning with cotton buds are ambiguous (see note below).

- Associated symptoms / review of systems (as mentioned):
  - No ear pain.
  - No ear discharge.
  - No fever reported.
  - No chest pain, no palpitations reported.
  - Mild dizziness / lightheadedness with occasional nausea; not severe or true vertigo.

- Pertinent negatives:
  - No documented focal neurological deficits.
  - No documented otorrhea, otalgia, fever.
  - No medications, allergies, smoking, alcohol, substance use, or family history documented in the visit.

- Not reported / not documented in transcript.

- No medications or allergies documented in the transcript.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded in transcript.
- Exam findings: No physical examination findings recorded. Plan made to perform in-person otoscopic ear exam.

- Plan documented in visit: in-person otoscopic examination of ears in clinic within ~4–5 days.

Assessment & Plan:
- Integrate transcript impressions with DDx insights: The clinician identified cerumen impaction as an initial, common and easily correctable cause to exclude first. The diagnostic reasoning (DDx) supports cerumen impaction as the highest-likelihood initial diagnosis, while also noting sensorineural etiologies (vestibular schwannoma, viral cochleitis/labyrinthitis, Meniere) as mid/low-likelihood alternatives to consider if otoscopy is normal.

Issue 1: Left-sided hearing loss with unilateral tinnitus
- Assessment:
  - Unilateral (left) decreased hearing for ~6 weeks with intermittent tinnitus. Conductive cause from cerumen impaction is the leading initial consideration (clinician explicitly suspected this), but sensorineural causes remain possible.
- Plan:
  - Book face-to-face clinic appointment within ~4–5 days for otoscopic examination to evaluate for impacted cerumen or visible middle/inner ear pathology (action documented by clinician).
  - If cerumen impaction is present: perform ear wax removal in clinic (standard next step; clinician implied removal if identified).
  - If otoscopy is normal (no obstructing wax/visible middle ear pathology): arrange further evaluation (audiometry and ENT referral and/or neuroimaging such as MRI if clinically indicated) to distinguish sensorineural causes (recommendation supported by DDx; to be pursued after otoscopy).
  - Provide tinnitus information leaflet (clinician to paste link in notes); patient advised to read about tinnitus and treatment options.

Issue 2: Intermittent mild dizziness / lightheadedness with nausea
- Assessment:
  - Mild, non-rotational imbalance symptoms temporally associated with ear symptoms. Not described as severe vertigo. No chest pain or palpitations reported.
- Plan:
  - Reassess vestibular symptoms at the in-person visit after otoscopic exam.
  - If ear exam normal and symptoms persist/worse: consider vestibular investigations/ENT assessment per standard practice (supported by DDx considerations such as vestibular schwannoma, labyrinthitis).
  - Patient advised to contact/support team or rebook if symptoms worsen prior to clinic appointment (clinician advice documented).

Issue 3: Tinnitus (left)
- Assessment:
  - Subjective tinnitus of the left ear, intermittent, masked by external sound.
- Plan:
  - Provide educational leaflet on tinnitus (clinician to paste link).
  - Discuss conservative management options after initial ear exam and any subsequent audiometry results.
  - No pharmacologic treatment initiated during this visit.

General / administrative plan items (from transcript):
- Clinician will message admin to schedule patient into an in-person ear clinic within ~4–5 days.
- Patient instructed to ring support team (number to be left in notes) to be slotted into clinic.
- Visit will likely be with another GP; clinician will leave notes and question for them to examine the ear.
- Not considered an emergency at this time; if problems arise before the clinic appointment, patient advised to book another appointment or contact clinician team.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Cerumen (earwax) impaction / obstructive conductive hearing loss
  - Likelihood: High
  - Rationale: Unilateral muffled hearing without pain or discharge, clinician explicitly suspected impacted wax as the first-line cause, tinnitus that can be masked by external sound is compatible with conductive pathology.
- Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Rationale: Classic fit with unilateral progressive hearing loss, unilateral tinnitus, and imbalance; warrants audiometry and possible imaging if otoscopy and initial testing do not demonstrate a conductive cause.
- Viral cochleitis / labyrinthitis (or other inner-ear inflammatory causes)
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Rationale: Unilateral hearing change with tinnitus and intermittent dizziness could reflect inner-ear inflammation; lack of pain/fever makes acute bacterial otitis less likely, but viral/inflammatory inner-ear causes remain possible and should be considered after exclusion of obstruction.
